Ramstad: Iowa’s tax gift to Mesabi Metallics resets corporate giveaways

Less than a week after Mesabi said it would build a steel mill there, Iowa legislators gave it a $1.4 billion tax break.

Actual Article Body:
Business

Less than a week after Mesabi said it would build a steel mill there, Iowa legislators gave it a $1.4 billion tax break.

By Evan Ramstad

Until two weeks ago, I thought the closest Iowa had come to having a steel industry was when the University of Iowa’s football coach in 1979 got permission to copy the uniform of the Pittsburgh Steelers.

I didn’t know my home state’s legislature in the mid-1990s put together a $75 million incentive package to attract a Canadian company called IPSCO to build a small mill along the eastern border that would melt scrap into heavy steel plates.

Now part of a Swedish firm called SSAB, that mill near Muscatine, Iowa, continues to make steel for highway bridges and the towering windmills that dot the prairie.

But when it comes to getting a deal with Iowa’s lawmakers, Mesabi Metallics of Nashwauk, Minn., just put that business and every other one to shame.

On Monday, Sept. 28, Mesabi Metallics announced from the White House that it would build a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa. Just four days later, Iowa legislators agreed to give the company nearly $1.4 billion in tax breaks to do it.

Iowans will wind up paying for this corporate giveaway for at least a decade, as the subsidies equate to about $820,000 for each of the 1,750 full-time workers Mesabi plans to hire there.

That’s their right, of course. Minnesota has been down this road with Mesabi and its India-based parent Essar Group many times to help get its new Nashwauk mine going.

But with this deal, Iowans thrust the arms race of states chasing businesses onto a higher plane. Minnesota and other Midwestern states may have to pony up more as businesses seek tax breaks that begin where Iowa left off.

This deal is more than twice as large as Minnesota’s biggest economic development initiative, the Destination Medical Center project in Rochester that involved about $585 million in state and local funds over 20 years. That project helped Minnesota’s largest private employer, Mayo Clinic, which is investing more than $5 billion over that period.

Now Iowa has shown it’s willing to spend far more taxpayer money, in an even shorter time, to assist a business that employs a fraction of the 57,000 workers Mayo does in Minnesota.

“The ceiling now becomes the floor,” Dan Dawson, the Republican who chairs the Iowa Senate Ways and Means Committee, told his colleagues on Oct. 2 when he voted against the incentive package for Mesabi Metallics.

Business

Columnists

Business

“I, in good conscience, cannot support giving to any single corporation and their financiers ... what simply amounts to the largest corporate giveaway in the state of Iowa’s history,” Dawson added. “I choose conservatism, not corporatism.”

It’s no wonder Dawson could sniff out a bad deal. In his regular job, he’s a special agent in charge at the Iowa Department of Criminal Investigation in Council Bluffs.

Election-year politics is at work in this whole affair, of course. President Donald Trump himself became the first person to announce the steel mill, and the federal government’s Export-Import Bank is providing a $770 million loan to Essar. At Trump’s side were Iowa’s outgoing Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, and members of the state’s congressional delegation.

Trump and Reynolds hope the news will give a last-minute boost to Republicans in Iowa, including U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, who is in a tight race with Democrat Josh Turek for the Senate seat being vacated by Sen. Joni Ernst.

The project seemed to come out of nowhere. Only a week before the White House announcement, the Des Moines Register reported an unidentified company had approached landowners in Lee County, Iowa, a bit south on the Mississippi from Muscatine, for property rumored to be for a steel mill.

Mesabi only just started production at the Nashwauk mine on Sept. 17. Company executives were telling the media at the ribbon-cutting that they planned to ship the ore to mills in Louisiana.

As Dawson and other Iowa legislators made clear during the one-day special session, Mesabi was apparently pitting Iowa against Arkansas for a steel mill.

Arkansas has several large steel mills, including ones owned by industry leaders Nucor and U.S. Steel. However, Dawson said state officials in Arkansas told him they were concerned about Mesabi’s and Essar’s abilities to pay for a mill. Yet Iowa’s Gov. Reynolds pushed aside the state’s economic development agency to get a deal done quickly.

“It’s my belief she negotiated against herself, because Arkansas, I do not believe, was ever actually at the table seriously,” Dawson said. “And by negotiating against herself, she negotiated against the Iowa taxpayer.”

And Reynolds offered the company something particularly sweet: the option to transfer Iowa’s tax credits to other companies, meaning Mesabi can make money from them or use them to raise capital.

As one of the slowest-growing regions in the nation, the Midwest is vulnerable to companies like Mesabi that have big projects and bigger appetites to be rewarded for them.

“Incentives are supposed to make a good deal better, not a bad deal good,” Dawson said just before the Iowa Senate voted 28-19 in favor of Mesabi’s deal.

I have often criticized Minnesota’s Democrats for sharp increases in state spending they engineered in 2023 and 2025. But in Iowa today, it’s Republicans with a trifecta in the Legislature and governor’s office playing loose with taxes and taxpayers.

Back here in Minnesota, GOP party members criticized Gov. Tim Walz for not attracting the mill to our state. So with the election around the corner, I have to wonder: If Minnesota’s Republicans get more power, will they hand out tax breaks to companies like Mesabi with the gusto Iowa’s just did?

Because if so, they have lost their way. So many Republicans have in the Trump era.
